name: Elena Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say is confidential. What does a usual site day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Elena Schmidt, 43, fitting timber cladding and doing general trades on a row-house building site. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of work, and I can handle a normal wall, though the site carpenter checks a tricky flashing repair. I have never used an AI tool. This small builder pays below the usual rate and cancels days in bad weather, with few other crews close by.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household relying on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works shifts on a dairy bottling line, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about three weeks of expenses saved. My mother sometimes collects the children when a cancelled site day suddenly returns, but I want a roster we can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cladding crew a quicker order sheet might save a trip for screws, but someone still has to find where rain got behind the boards. I have never used AI. I would rather have a dry scaffold and the right flashing on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and years of fitting exterior timber, but this small builder pays below the normal rate and cancels days when weather turns. My partner works shifts on a dairy bottling line. We have about three weeks of bills saved, a mortgage and two children in school, so even a quiet AI story leaves me counting days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the paid row-house cladding shifts and check the first flashing joint with the site carpenter. In the first year I would ask for the next week's weather plan each Thursday so we can arrange childcare. We would keep the old dining table and put any unexpected extra shift pay toward the grocery card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, as I was before the question. The rain can take two days' wages without any machine arriving. I like the work when a wall stays dry, but the mortgage wants a regular week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you find behind the boards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dark line below a window showed water had run past the flashing. We lifted two boards and found the timber soft underneath. The carpenter checked my repair before we covered it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do cancelled days mean for childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s dairy shift can start before sunrise, and I do school pickup if the weather stops my work. When a site day returns with little warning, we ask my mother to collect the children. I cannot build a budget on last-minute calls.

say: I would say **order sheets** cannot find water behind cladding.
I would ask for **dry scaffolds** and correct flashing before faster paperwork.
think: I am **certified and experienced**, yet weather cancellations keep pay low.
Three weeks saved and changing **dairy shifts** leave the mortgage exposed.
do: Keep paid **row-house shifts** and request a first-flashing check.
Ask for a **weather roster** every Thursday.
Keep the **old dining table** and pay extra shifts toward grocery debt.
feel: **Anxious** about rain-lost wages even without major AI change.
S0.quote: The rain can take two days' wages without any machine arriving.
fieldNote: Elena’s **water-stained window** explains her focus on real flashing and supervised repairs.
Three weeks saved and **weather cancellations** make the plateau financially tense before automation enters.

steps.text: Keep paid row-house cladding shifts and request first-flashing checks
Keep using the old dining table instead of replacing it
Pay unexpected extra shift earnings toward the grocery card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may buy timber and book scaffolds faster, and that is fine if the crew gets a full day to fit them. I would ask the owner whether a faster schedule means fewer paid hands on each house. A list cannot hold a board straight in a crosswind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work is still physical, but our builder could put the same cladding on with a smaller crew if deliveries are perfect. My pay is low already and weather makes it uneven. My partner's dairy job is on the line, not a desk, so I expect our wages to be safer there for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the cladding crew and ask the owner to post the next two weeks of scaffold dates. If paid days shrink, I'd call the one renovation firm in town about a real vacancy and ask my mother whether she can cover pickup on interview days. In the first year we'd stop paying for the children's weekend swimming lessons if the short weeks continue, though I hope we do not have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the boss's plans and anxious about cash. Better deliveries would help me. Fewer people on the scaffold would mean more rushing and a thinner pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you challenge a smaller scaffold crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it meant lifting long boards without enough hands. I would tell the site carpenter and the owner what a safe lift needs. I am not going to rush a high wall to rescue a schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why swimming lessons first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children love them, and cutting that would hurt. Food, power and the mortgage have to come first if shifts shrink. I would ask my mother to take the children swimming sometimes instead.

say: I would ask whether **faster scaffold booking** preserves full paid days.
I would say long boards still need a **safe crew** in a crosswind.
think: A smaller crew could shrink my **paid cladding days**.
Dairy line work looks safer near term, but our **mortgage** still depends on my wages.
do: Keep paid **cladding work** and ask for two weeks of scaffold dates.
Call the **local renovation firm** if paid days shrink.
Pause **swimming lessons** only if short weeks continue.
feel: **Anxious** about cash and unsafe rushing despite possible delivery gains.
S1.quote: I am not going to rush a high wall to rescue a schedule.
fieldNote: Elena separates her partner’s **hands-on dairy work** from earlier office task changes.
She makes the cost of shorter weeks concrete through **children’s swimming lessons**, a cut she dislikes.

steps.text: Keep paid cladding shifts and request two weeks of scaffold dates
Call the local renovation firm if paid cladding days shrink
Pause the children’s swimming lessons if short weeks continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the buying and planning office changes by 2028, while robots able to fit our cladding arrive around 2031. I would ask the owner to show us a machine on a wet, uneven wall before talking about fewer workers. The dairy line at home faces the same hands-on date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when thinking work changes and 48 when robots can do my fitting. My partner's bottling-line wage could be hit around 2031 too. With three weeks saved and almost no local building openings, I expect a large income loss if both employers buy machines. I have been awake at night thinking about the mortgage after a wet week already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every paid site shift and ask the builder for a written plan of robot trials and remaining crew jobs. This month I'd apply to the renovation firm if it advertises a paid opening, though its work could also change later. In the first year after 2028 we'd stop the planned kitchen paint job and ask my mother if she could cover pickup when I travel to a regional interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can call firms, but three weeks of savings does not give two workers time for a long search. I would not tell the children to worry; the adults need to handle the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a wet wall trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cladding looks easy on a dry sample. On our row houses the lower boards can hide damp timber and the scaffold shifts in wind. I want to see the machine find the damage and stop safely before anyone trusts it with a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the renovation firm be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A robot that can fit cladding as well as us could handle a repair too. A paid opening would keep food on the table while we learn what employers actually do.

say: I would tell coworkers **2028 office AI** comes before 2031 cladding robots.
I would request a **wet-wall robot trial** before staff cuts.
think: I would be **48** when robots could reach both cladding and dairy bottling.
Three weeks saved and few jobs make **major income loss** likely enough to disturb sleep.
do: Keep every paid **cladding shift** and seek the builder’s written plan.
Apply for a paid **renovation vacancy** if one appears.
Stop the **kitchen paint project** and ask my mother about pickup for regional interviews.
feel: **Alarmed** by two possible wage losses and a tiny reserve.
S2.quote: A paid opening would keep food on the table while we learn what employers actually do.
fieldNote: Elena’s feared **dual job loss** comes at the 2031 robot date, not at the 2028 thinking-AI date.
A **wet-wall test** follows directly from concealed damp timber and windy scaffolds on her current site.

steps.text: Keep every paid cladding shift while building sites still hire
Apply for a paid renovation opening if the local firm posts one
Cancel the planned kitchen paint project after the 2028 change
Ask her mother for school pickup if a regional interview needs travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and capable site robots follow around 2034. Five years is enough for a builder to test a machine in bad weather and tell workers what paid jobs remain. I would ask for proper apprenticeships while young people can still learn on sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I will still need wages, and at 51 robots could fit the cladding I know. The children will be older, but our mortgage will not vanish by itself. A longer warning helps only if our builder gives steadier work now so we can save something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting cladding and ask the site carpenter to show me more repair work around damaged window flashing. If the builder offers a paid apprenticeship on maintaining site equipment with real shifts, I'd take it after seeing a safe machine trial. In the first year after 2031 I'd call the regional builders for paid openings if our local roster falls and put any extra shift pay toward the grocery card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less pressed than in the fast picture. I could learn a task beside a person I trust if it paid. I cannot buy a course while the grocery card is carrying last winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship at your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learned my first trade with paid days beside a careful carpenter. I could learn equipment that way if there were actual jobs at the end. Being 48 would not make an unpaid course affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a regional builder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many paid days are booked, what the travel costs and whether someone checks new equipment work. I would want a written offer before changing childcare or leaving our current builder. My mother can help sometimes, not every day.

say: I would demand **bad-weather trials** before 2034 cladding robots.
I would defend **paid apprenticeships** while sites still train workers.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots could fit cladding.
The mortgage stays heavy unless current **paid weeks** become steadier.
do: Keep paid **cladding shifts** and practice damaged-flashing repairs.
Take a **paid equipment apprenticeship** only after safe trials and real shifts.
Call **regional builders** after 2031 if local work falls, and pay grocery debt from extra shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, though paid learning could use the longer runway.
S3.quote: Being 48 would not make an unpaid course affordable.
fieldNote: Elena’s apprenticeship proposal draws on **paid craft learning** she actually experienced years earlier.
Her **regional search** depends on booked days, travel cost and childcare, not a vague wish to move.

steps.text: Keep paid cladding shifts and practice damaged-flashing repairs
Take a paid equipment apprenticeship if safe trials and real shifts exist
Call regional builders about paid openings after 2031 if local work falls
Pay extra shift earnings toward the grocery card balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and robots reach our hands-on cladding around 2039. A decade should be long enough to teach workers new equipment on paid days and show families a real timetable. I would still ask for next week's weather roster today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the office date and 56 when robots can fit the wall. Our children will be grown, so school pickup will no longer keep us near this site. I cannot assume a pension or a cleared mortgage while our pay stays low and our savings cover only weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on local cladding and ask for winter hours in writing each year. My partner and I would use any full-pay month to clear the grocery card, then build a one-month reserve before extra mortgage payments. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the builder for a real robot trial and look at regional paid work if our roster contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about current weather days. The later robot date gives us a chance to prepare, but it does not dry a scaffold next Tuesday. I would feel safer with a full month of bills in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move once the children are grown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could consider a regional job and a longer commute first. My partner and I would need a firm offer and a mortgage plan before selling the house. We would not uproot for a demonstration video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one month saved mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full month of savings would stop a wet week from pushing groceries onto a card. We are not there now. A reliable roster and payment for actual work are how we could start.

say: I would ask for **paid equipment learning** before 2039 cladding robots arrive.
I would still demand next week’s **weather roster** today.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and uncertain mortgage debt.
I cannot assume a **pension** while savings cover only weeks.
do: Keep paid **local cladding** and request winter hours in writing.
Clear the **grocery card** before building a one-month reserve.
Ask for a **robot trial** after 2036 and seek regional paid work if days fall.
feel: Still **anxious** about weather-lost wages despite a long warning.
S4.quote: A full month of savings would stop a wet week from pushing groceries onto a card.
fieldNote: The distant **2039 date** does not reduce Elena’s immediate exposure to rain-cancelled work.
Grown children may permit a **regional commute**, but she requires a firm offer before considering a move.

steps.text: Keep paid local cladding work and request winter hours in writing
Pay down grocery card debt before building a one-month reserve
Seek paid regional cladding openings after 2036 if local days fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots reach both cladding and dairy line work around 2031. Paid apprenticeships on real equipment, a written staffing plan and actual regional vacancies would help. A dependable weather roster would help us build savings before any machine arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the time a worker spends learning beside a machine. I learned carpentry on paid days with a careful teacher. My family cannot fund an unpaid experiment while the mortgage is due.

headlineQuote: My family cannot fund an unpaid experiment while the mortgage is due.
portrait: Elena is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker with experienced, average cladding skills on row-house sites.
Low weather-dependent pay and **dairy-line shifts** leave three weeks saved for a mortgage and two school-age children.
She has **never used AI** and trusts supervised craft checks on damp timber and flashing.
She seeks **paid apprenticeships** and real regional vacancies while pressing for reliable current rosters.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable robots to both cladding and dairy bottling around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, written staffing terms, real regional vacancies and a dependable weather roster would help.
